work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [He said] that, on the apostle’s testimony, marital chastity is God’s gift.
translator_notes: Julian cites Augustine’s statement approvingly; its scriptural basis is 1 Corinthians 7:7. Augustine’s own source is On Marriage and Concupiscence 1.3.3.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [They are] prepared for the devil’s kingdom.
translator_notes: Julian’s accusation about the implications of Augustine’s teaching for newborn children. Augustine rejects this as the purpose of procreation. The “army of the apostles” phrase later in the section repeats Against Julian 3.26.65.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Marital intercourse was devised by the devil.
The union of bodies arose through the evil of transgression.
translator_notes: Julian attributes these claims to Augustine; Augustine explicitly denies them.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: It follows that God’s gift causes harm if a human being is born with evil, since no one is born except by God’s gift.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: We should pray for the power to have intercourse.
translator_notes: Julian takes this to follow from Augustine’s teaching that marital goodness should be sought from God. Augustine says that he meant chastity, not sexual capacity.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: I will strike at the other side of [his] definition.

If sexual warmth, the servant of honorable marriage, is restrained from excessive outbursts both by the effort of believers and by the power of the gift, and is curbed rather than extinguished by grace, it is commendable in its kind and within its proper measure; only its excesses are blameworthy.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If sexual warmth could be evil by nature, it should be rooted out, not regulated.
translator_notes: Augustine contrasts Julian’s word “regulated” here with “curbed” in the preceding fragment.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [It should] be entirely removed by the mind’s effort. This should have happened if it were evil.
translator_notes: Julian’s challenge concerning sexual desire. Augustine embeds these two short quotations in his response.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Moderating a thing that harms by its very nature does nothing to advance innocence.
Desire produces seed.
translator_notes: The first is Julian’s objection to Augustine’s distinction between desire and its restrained use. The second is a short phrase quoted within Augustine’s reply.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [Thanks should be given for] either the control or the origin [of desire].
translator_notes: Augustine quotes these terms separately and together while distinguishing gratitude for controlling desire from gratitude for its origin. Brackets supply that setting rather than invent a complete recovered sentence.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: I pursue the points [in his argument] that seem clever to him.
Eagerly blaming the substance, [he] praises its gifts.
translator_notes: Julian criticizes Augustine’s account of human nature. “Substance” means human nature itself. The long quotations elsewhere in this section are Augustine’s own earlier statements, not new fragments of Julian.
Review clarification: “seem clever to him” preserves Augustine’s own self-assessment within Julian’s reported criticism.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [A person is helped] to attain perfection.
A human being is stirred toward something praiseworthy by the impulses of a noble heart.
Human nature is good, since it deserves the help of such grace.
[I thought he called] the achievement of the human will heavenly gifts.
translator_notes: These are separated parts of Julian’s discussion of grace and human willing. Augustine disputes the implication that a good will begins independently of grace.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: People outside the faith abound in virtues. In them there is only the good of nature, without the help of grace, although that nature is enslaved to superstitions. Through the powers of inborn freedom alone they are often found to be merciful, modest, chaste, and sober.
translator_notes: In the following section Augustine names Julian’s examples: Fabricius, Fabius, Scipio, and Regulus. They are Roman historical figures, not biblical figures.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Scripture Julian uses, as reported by Augustine
english: “Everyone who competes in a contest exercises self-restraint in everything” (1 Corinthians 9:25).
translator_notes: Augustine reports that Julian used this verse to argue that flute players and similar performers can possess self-restraint. Only the cited biblical wording is reproduced here; Augustine’s reply supplies the rest of the context.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The origin of every virtue lies in the rational soul. All the dispositions through which we are good, either fruitfully or fruitlessly, have their foundation in our mind: prudence, justice, self-control, and courage. Although the power of these dispositions is naturally present in everyone, it does not hasten toward the same goal in everyone. Instead, according to the judgment of the will whose direction they obey, they are directed either toward eternal things or toward temporary things. When this happens, they differ neither in what they are nor in what they do, but only in what they deserve. They therefore cannot suffer any loss of their name or their kind; they are simply enriched by the greatness of the reward they sought, or disappointed by its smallness.
translator_notes: Augustine repeats the closing distinction later in the section, and the opening “fruitfully or fruitlessly” statement at 4.3.22. His quotations from other classical writers are his own replies, not part of Julian’s preserved passage.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Scripture Julian uses, as reported by Augustine
english: “Gentiles who do not have the law are a law to themselves. They have the work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans 2:14–15).
“They naturally do what the law requires” (Romans 2:14).
translator_notes: Augustine identifies these as the passages Julian used to support the possibility of genuine righteousness among people outside Christian faith. His objection and the additional verses he introduces belong to Augustine.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23).
translator_notes: Augustine reports that Julian understood this statement in its immediate context about food, rather than as a judgment on every act of unbelievers. No complete verbatim statement of Julian’s explanation is given here.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Will those in whom there was true righteousness therefore be in everlasting condemnation?

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If someone says that the chastity of unbelievers is not chastity, with the same shamelessness one will say that pagans’ bodies are not bodies, that pagans’ eyes have no power to see, and that grain growing in pagans’ fields is not grain—and many other things so absurd that they can make people who understand laugh.

“The soul and body, and every good thing naturally implanted in soul and body, are God’s gifts even in sinners, since God made these things, not they themselves. But of the things they do it was said: Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23).
translator_notes: The second paragraph is Augustine’s own sentence, which he explicitly says Julian included in his book; it is retained as a quoted source in Julian’s argument, not as Julian’s own position. Augustine’s later repetition of it is omitted.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: I am amazed that such an outstanding intellect did not see how much he helped us in this too, when he said: “Some sins are overcome by other sins.”
Therefore a human being can very easily be free from sins through the pursuit of holiness, which God assists. For if sins are overcome by sins, how much more can sins be overcome by virtues?
translator_notes: The opening is Julian’s sarcasm about Augustine. Augustine repeats the second statement at 4.3.29.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If a pagan clothes a naked person, is it a sin because it is not from faith?
If a pagan clothes a naked person, rescues someone in danger, tends a sick person’s wounds, spends their wealth in honorable friendship, and cannot be forced even by torture to give false testimony…
translator_notes: The second excerpt expands the first example; Augustine interrupts it with questions, so it is not given an invented conclusion. These examples resemble biblical duties such as Isaiah 58:7 and Matthew 25:35–36, and the prohibition of false witness in Exodus 20:16. They also belong to broader moral teaching, so specific allusions cannot be established from this wording alone.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Children are under the devil’s power because they are born from the union of bodies.
translator_notes: Julian attributes this to Augustine. Augustine distinguishes “children who are born from bodily union” from “children are under the devil because of bodily union,” denying the latter.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Since we are composed of unequal goods, the soul ought to rule the body. We share the one with the gods and the other with beasts. Therefore the better part—the soul endowed with virtue—rightly commands both the body’s members and its desires.
translator_notes: Augustine reports and quotes Julian’s argument in the language of classical philosophy. “The gods” preserves the plural in this argument; it should not be silently rewritten as a Christian confession of multiple gods. The phrase recalls Sallust, The War with Catiline 1.2.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [He has said], in a ridiculous contradiction, that some are guilty from a good act and others holy from an evil act.
“Unbelievers turn the good of marriage into evil and sin by using it without faith; in the same way, believers’ marriages turn the evil of desire to a righteous use.”
translator_notes: The second paragraph is the statement by Augustine that Julian criticizes in the first. Augustine denies that Julian’s reconstruction follows from it.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If someone could be created evil, they could never pass into goodness through washing.
translator_notes: “Washing” refers to baptism.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Demons instituted marriage.
[They instituted] the union of seed between the two sexes.
Marital intercourse for the purpose of conceiving children is the devil’s work.
Demons would catch married people in intercourse and, finding them engaged in their own work, would not allow them to conceive children who were to be freed by rebirth.
translator_notes: Julian argues that these consequences follow from Augustine’s view; Augustine denies the premises. The last is Julian’s hypothetical scenario, not a claim that such an encounter actually happened.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Adultery and other sexual wrongdoing should therefore be committed so that children may be conceived.
translator_notes: An absurd consequence Julian says follows from Augustine’s position; neither writer endorses it.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Under the name of grace, [they say] that people become good through the necessity of fate.
translator_notes: Julian’s characterization of Augustine’s side, rejected by Augustine. The separate formulation about grace being given according to merits is attributed broadly to the Pelagian party in the response; it is not a new literal Julian fragment here.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [He says] that no effort should be expected from the human will, contrary to the Gospel, where the Lord says: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:7–8).
translator_notes: Julian’s accusation against Augustine. The wording also occurs in Luke 11:9–10.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [The door is opened to those who knock by him] “who wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4).
translator_notes: Augustine reports Julian’s connection between the promise to those who knock (Matthew 7:7–8; Luke 11:9–10) and the verse from 1 Timothy. The supplied connection is bracketed because Augustine does not give it as a continuous literal quotation.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: What does not happen on the basis of merit happens by fate.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Free will is denied if grace is praised; and, in turn, grace is denied if free will is praised.
When those books themselves begin to be examined, the ungodliness of those statements will be exposed and pierced.
translator_notes: The first is Julian’s report of Augustine’s On the Grace of Christ 1.47.52. Augustine protests that Julian removed the qualifying words “seems” and “is thought”: Augustine had described an apparent difficulty, not declared an actual contradiction. The second is Julian’s promise to examine those writings.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: It contributes nothing to the praise of grace if it gives its own people what sins bestow on the ungodly.
translator_notes: The subject is marital chastity, which Julian argues can also be found outside Christian faith.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The joining of married people’s sexual organs is evil.
Its offense goes unpunished through religion.
“Let us do evil so that good may come” (Romans 3:8).
In Christian spouses, do you call the pleasure of intercourse chastity or unchastity?
translator_notes: The first two statements are Julian’s charges about Augustine’s teaching; Augustine rejects them. Julian invokes the saying in Romans as a criticism of the position, not as a command he endorses.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If, because of this evil of desire, guilty offspring are brought forth even from Christian spouses, it follows that virgin chastity brings happiness. And since it is found among the ungodly, unbelievers raised high by the virtue of chastity surpass Christians polluted by the stain of desire.
Among them, faith allows crime to go unpunished.
translator_notes: Julian argues against what he takes to be the consequences of Augustine’s view. Augustine denies both the premise about genuine chastity among unbelievers and the charge of impunity.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If someone commits murder while their conscience is afraid, they are guilty because they were afraid. But if they commit some crime with triumphant boldness, as though believing that they do their evil deed from faith, they escape guilt.
translator_notes: Julian attributes this teaching to the Manichaeans in order to criticize Augustine’s view of faith. Augustine says he has never heard the Manichaeans teach it and denies that the catholic faith teaches it. It is not Julian’s own moral position.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Natural desire is therefore good. When kept within its proper measure, it is stained by no taint of evil.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: “Were not the first spouses, whose marriage God blessed by saying, ‘Increase and multiply’ (Genesis 1:28), naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:25)? Why, then, did shame about those organs follow sin, unless an indecent movement arose there, which marriage would certainly not have had if human beings had not sinned?”
translator_notes: Augustine explicitly identifies these as his own words quoted and challenged by Julian.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: In the fact that the first human beings, ashamed after their sin, covered the organs where desire is present, [he] found a way to persuade people that God had established marriages made of air.
[That] without which nature does not exist is not natural.
translator_notes: The first phrase mocks Augustine’s account of marriage before sin; it refers to Genesis 3:7. The second is Julian’s characterization of Augustine’s denial that present sexual desire belonged to original human nature. Augustine rejects both characterizations. “Marriages made of air” means marriages lacking bodily reality.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [His] position is a bedbug: alive it causes trouble, and crushed it gives off a stench.
[I am] ashamed to crush him by defeating him.
As though defeated, [he has] fled to filthy places, and [I] recoil from following and killing him.
Because [I am] forced to speak about the sexual organs, [my] modesty, like a temple keeper, has excluded from free expression the parts of [my] argument that would crush or destroy him.
translator_notes: Augustine breaks up Julian’s imagery with his own comments; the fragments are kept separate and changes of grammatical person are bracketed. This is polemical imagery about debating, not a threat of physical violence.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If there is no marriage without desire, and you condemn desire in general, you condemn marriage too.
That without which marriage does not exist cannot be called a disease. Marriage can exist apart from sin; but the apostle calls disease sin.
translator_notes: Julian is pressing the consequences of calling desire a disease. Augustine’s response cites the “disease of desire” in 1 Thessalonians 4:4–5; the surviving excerpt does not specify which Pauline wording Julian had in mind.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Balbus, in Cicero, discussed the matter truthfully and carefully with Cotta.
[I quote] a few things to increase his shame: under the teaching of the sacred law he has failed to understand things that pagans could grasp through reason alone.
[Balbus] touches on the working of the sexes under the subject of animals because, for the sake of propriety, he passed over it in describing human beings.

[He] portrays the human being in words: the stomach lies below the gullet as a receptacle for food and drink; the lungs and heart draw breath from outside; many things in the stomach are wonderfully fashioned from sinews; its many folds and windings hold and contain what it receives, whether dry or liquid.
[The remaining food is expelled] as the intestines alternately contract and relax.
translator_notes: Julian uses Cicero’s On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2, to argue that covering a bodily part need not imply shame from sin. Augustine quotes pieces and summarizes others; brackets identify necessary connections in this interrupted witness. The physiology belongs to the ancient text. Augustine’s own additional comparison about disagreeable speech is not included as Julian’s wording.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Our Maker himself acknowledged no fault in his craftsmanship when he hid our vital organs so carefully.
So that they would neither perish nor cause horror if exposed.
translator_notes: Julian’s point is that organs can be hidden for protection or to avoid an unpleasant sight, without implying moral evil. The second fragment gives the purpose of their concealment.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [I ask] modest ears to forgive [me], and to share [my] distress rather than be indignant at [my] necessity.
If the male organ could move before, then sin introduced nothing new.
translator_notes: Julian apologizes for speaking about sexual organs while disputing Augustine’s account of Genesis 3:7. The exact grammatical person of Augustine’s embedded report is adjusted in brackets.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: If this desire was in the fruit of that tree, it is shown to have been made by God and is therefore defended as good as well.
translator_notes: The forbidden tree in Genesis 2:16–17 and Genesis 3:1–7. This is a conditional objection; Julian does not affirm that desire was literally inside the fruit.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: When the apostle John said, “Everything in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition, which is not from the Father but from the world” (1 John 2:16), he was not condemning this world—that is, heaven and earth and all the things that substantially exist in it, the world made by the Father through the Son.
[The desire of the flesh that is not from the Father] should be understood as excess.
translator_notes: The first passage gives Julian’s distinction, repeated by Augustine as a point they agree on. The second gives his reading of “desire of the flesh.” “Excess” renders luxuria: disordered self-indulgence rather than the mere existence of desire. Later imagined answers supplied by Augustine are omitted.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: It follows that we must confess that our senses of sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch were given to us by the devil rather than by God, if we concede that the desire of the flesh against which we struggle through self-restraint was not in paradise before sin, but arose from the first sin which the devil persuaded the first human being to commit.
translator_notes: Julian presents this as an unacceptable consequence of Augustine’s view, not as his own account of the senses.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Let drunkenness not condemn wine, or overeating condemn food, or obscenity discredit desire.
Its excess is blameworthy.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Imitating animals is always sinful.
translator_notes: Augustine identifies this as a position Julian argued against, and denies that it was the position he had put forward. Augustine also reports that Julian collected examples of animal behavior followed by medical practice, but he does not preserve those individual examples here.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: All the philosophers who tried to work out anything about the causes of natural things—even though they taught otherwise in their schools yet worshiped idols with the common people—have nevertheless touched, as it were, some parts of truth amid the many empty notions in their thinking. Empty though they are through their darkness, they can rightly be preferred to this doctrine we are opposing.
Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages; then Anaximander, Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Parmenides, Leucippus, Democritus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, Melissus, Plato, and the Pythagoreans.
translator_notes: Augustine says Julian accompanied these names with their different accounts of nature, but he does not preserve those accounts here. The list and Julian’s introductory claim are retained without inventing the missing exposition.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: It is now time to show, beyond nature’s testimony, by some authority of the sacred law as well, that our members were formed so that some enjoy modesty and others freedom. To confirm this, let the Teacher of the Gentiles be summoned, who says in writing to the Corinthians: “Our body is not one member, but many” (1 Corinthians 12:14).
Since he had named a few members of the whole body, and out of his own propriety did not wish to name the sexual organs directly…
translator_notes: Augustine says Julian continued with Paul’s account of the unity and agreement of the members (1 Corinthians 12:15–21), but does not reproduce it fully in this section. The second fragment is interrupted. “Teacher of the Gentiles” recalls 1 Timothy 2:7 and 2 Timothy 1:11.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: “Much more, the members of our body that seem weak are necessary. Those members of the body which we think less honorable we surround with greater honor; and our modest parts have greater dignity, while our presentable parts need nothing. But God has arranged the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it, so that there may be no division in the body, but its members may have the same care for one another” (1 Corinthians 12:22–25).
Look at the true interpreter of God’s work! Look at the faithful herald of his wisdom! “Our modest parts,” he says, “are covered with greater dignity.”
translator_notes: Augustine disputes the rendering “modest parts” in the Latin version Julian used, arguing that the Greek says “unpresentable parts.” This translation preserves Julian’s cited wording because that wording is central to his argument. It does not silently replace it with a modern Bible version.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Human beings were naked at first because making coverings for themselves was a task for human skill, which they did not yet possess.

It was not, therefore, because they had sinned that they made the sexual organs either diabolical or shameful. Rather, because they were afraid, they covered organs that remained in the same honorable condition in which they had first existed.
translator_notes: Julian’s interpretation of Genesis 2:25 and Genesis 3:7–10.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Why did Adam and his wife hide when they heard God walking in paradise, when those loincloths could have been enough if they had been ashamed of their naked sexual organs? (Genesis 3:7–10)

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: We must reject the opinion that the devil created anything in human beings’ members or in the senses of those members.
